meta.blurb: Before Columbus, millions of people farmed, built cities and shaped whole landscapes across two continents. Meet the Maya, the Inca, the Aztecs and many others, and learn how their world rose, flourished and was changed for ever.
meta.bible: The Americas: North America, Central America, South America, and the Caribbean. Columbus: Christopher Columbus, who reached the Bahamas in October 1492. Taino: the people he met first. Teosinte: the wild grass that became Maize. Cacao: source of Chocolate. Chuno: freeze-dried Andean Potatoes. Caral: city in the Supe valley of Peru, about 5,000 years old. Olmec: people of the Gulf of Mexico coast, about 3,000 years ago. Maya: classic cities such as Tikal, Palenque and Copan, about 250 to 900; Maya people live today. Teotihuacan: planned city near Mexico City, large by 500. Nazca, Moche: peoples of Peru. Inca: empire of Cusco under Pachacuti, called Tawantinsuyu; Chasqui runners; Quipu knotted cords; Mita labour tax; Machu Picchu, built about 1450. Huayna Capac, Atahualpa, Huascar: Inca ruler and his sons. Francisco Pizarro: arrived 1532. Aztecs or Mexica: founded Tenochtitlan about 1325 in Lake Texcoco; Tlatelolco market; Chinampas garden plots. Hernan Cortes: reached Tenochtitlan in 1519; the city fell in 1521. Cahokia: city near the Mississippi in Illinois, grew after 1050. Chaco Canyon: in New Mexico, ancestors of the Pueblo peoples. Haudenosaunee: confederacy of Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca; Great Law of Peace. Haida, Tlingit: peoples of the northwest coast; Potlatches. Inuit: peoples of the Arctic; Kayaks. Blackfoot, Pawnee: Great Plains peoples who hunted Bison. Amazon: Terra Preta, dark fertile soil. Norse: Vikings from Greenland who reached Newfoundland about 1000 at L'Anse aux Meadows. Quechua, Nahuatl, Guarani, Navajo: languages spoken today. Lidar: laser survey. Andes, Mexico, Peru, Guatemala, Brazil, Canada, Alaska, Oregon, Illinois, Egypt, Europe, Asia, Africa, Atlantic, Pacific, Arctic, Bahamas, Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, Chichen Itza, Cusco, Venus, Spanish, Italian, Indian, Indigenous, Native Americans. Voice and tone: wondering, clear and fair; the facts are real and hedged where scholars disagree; dates and numbers are approximate; no invented quotes; disease and conquest are stated plainly, without gore.

B1B2: When Columbus sailed across the Atlantic in 1492, the Americas were not an empty land. Tens of millions of people already lived there, and scholars still argue about the exact number.

The first people reached the Americas at least fifteen thousand years ago, and some finds suggest an earlier date. They came from Asia, at a time when the sea level was much lower because so much water was frozen.
Along the coast, the first travellers found fish, seals and shellfish, so they could keep moving south. Many scientists believe that boats helped them to travel much faster than they could on foot.

In those days, giant animals lived in the Americas, including mammoths, ground sloths and huge bears. Within a few thousand years most had vanished, and scientists think that climate change and hunting both played a part.

As the ice melted, people spread out and made their homes in forests, deserts, mountains and river valleys. Over time they came to speak hundreds of different languages, and no two peoples lived in quite the same way.

In Mexico, farmers took a wild grass called teosinte and slowly changed it into maize. By saving the seeds of the best plants again and again over thousands of years, they made the cobs bigger and richer.
Many farmers grew maize, beans and squash together in the same field. The beans climbed the maize stalks, and the wide squash leaves shaded the ground and kept weeds away.

The Americas gave the world potatoes, tomatoes, chillies, peanuts, sunflowers and cacao, which is the plant that chocolate comes from. Before 1492, none of these foods was grown in Europe, Africa or Asia.
In the Andes mountains, people kept llamas to carry loads and alpacas for their soft wool. There were no horses, cattle or sheep in the Americas, so most heavy work was done by people.

In the dry valley of Supe, in Peru, stand the ruins of Caral, a city about five thousand years old. It had huge stone platforms and plazas and was built around the time of the first Egyptian pyramids.

More than three thousand years ago, the Olmec people built towns on the hot, wet coast of the Gulf of Mexico. They carved giant stone heads, some of which are taller than a person and weigh many tonnes.

The people of Mexico and Central America made rubber from tree sap, long before Europeans had seen it. They used rubber balls in a fast game played in stone courts, which could also have a religious meaning.
The Maya built great cities in the rainforests of Mexico and Central America, such as Tikal. Their stone temples rose above the trees, and each city had its own king rather than one ruler for all.
The Maya wrote in picture-like signs and recorded history on stone and in folding books. They used zero in their counting, and they tracked the moon, the sun and the planet Venus very carefully.
Between about 800 and 900, many cities in the southern Maya lowlands lost their kings and slowly emptied. Scholars point to drought, war and damage to the land, but the Maya people did not vanish.
Near present-day Mexico City stood Teotihuacan, a planned city with a wide avenue and two giant pyramids. Around the year 500, it was probably one of the largest cities in the whole world.

In the dry desert of Peru, the Nazca people made giant pictures of birds and animals by moving dark stones. The pictures are so big that people can see them properly only from a high hill or an aircraft.

The Inca began as a small kingdom around the city of Cusco, high in the Andes mountains. Within about a hundred years, under rulers such as Pachacuti, they controlled the biggest empire in the Americas.
The Inca built a vast network of roads, with stone steps and rope bridges across deep valleys. Relay runners called chasqui carried messages from one station to the next, day and night.
The Inca had no alphabet, but they kept careful records with quipus, bundles of knotted strings. The position of each knot stood for a number, and trained officials could read them.
Around 1450, the Inca built Machu Picchu on a high mountain ridge, probably as a royal estate. The stones were cut so exactly that they fit together without any cement to hold them.
The Inca used no money of any kind, and people paid their taxes with work instead. Every family owed the state labour, and the state kept food in storehouses for hard times.
The Aztecs, who called themselves the Mexica, founded Tenochtitlan on an island in a lake around 1325. Long causeways joined the city to the shore, and canals ran between many of its streets.
To feed the city, farmers built small garden plots called chinampas in the shallow lake. They piled mud and plants into rectangles, and the rich wet soil gave them several harvests a year.
Merchants and shoppers crowded into the huge market at Tlatelolco, beside Tenochtitlan. Cacao beans worked almost like small coins, and buyers used them to pay for food and cloth.
In Aztec cities, most boys went to school, and many girls received some training as well. Noble families sent their sons to a separate school that trained leaders, priests and officials.

The Aztecs believed that the gods had sacrificed themselves to create the world and that people owed them a gift in return. This belief led to human sacrifice, which was real, though Spanish writers often exaggerated the numbers.

Near the Mississippi River, in the middle of North America, stood the city of Cahokia. Around 1100, thousands of people lived there, and its biggest mound was wider at the base than Egypt's Great Pyramid.

In Chaco Canyon, in the dry southwest of today's United States, ancestors of the Pueblo peoples built huge stone houses. Some had hundreds of rooms, and wide straight roads led away from the canyon into the desert.
In the forests of the northeast, five nations joined to form the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. Their Great Law of Peace explained how leaders from each nation would meet, talk and decide together.

On the northwest Pacific coast, people lived very well without farming, because the rivers were full of salmon. They built plank houses and canoes from cedar trees, and they carved tall poles that told family stories.
In the freezing Arctic, the Inuit and their ancestors hunted seals, whales and caribou. They made warm clothes from animal skins and light boats called kayaks, and some built shelters from snow.
On the Great Plains of North America, many peoples depended on the huge herds of bison. Before horses arrived from Europe, hunters on foot drove the animals into traps or over cliffs.

Many people once lived along the Amazon River, and they changed the forest to grow more food. They made rich, dark soil, called terra preta, by mixing charcoal, bones and broken pottery into the ground.
In many places, people lit small, careful fires to clear the ground and help useful plants grow. The young grass that sprang up afterwards attracted deer and other animals, so hunting was easier.

Goods travelled thousands of kilometres across the Americas, passed from one trader to the next. Turquoise from the southwest, shells from the sea and cacao from the tropics all reached distant places.
In the cold Andes, people made a food called chuno from potatoes. They let the potatoes freeze at night and dry in the sun by day, and the result could be kept for years.

Farmers needed to know the right time to plant, so many peoples watched the sky with great care. They built towers and stone markers that lined up with the sun on the longest and shortest days of the year.
Craftspeople in the Americas made beautiful objects from a wide range of materials. They wove fine cloth, shaped gold into jewellery and made bright pictures from tropical feathers.

The Americas held empires, confederacies, city-kingdoms and small bands of hunters, all living side by side. Each people had its own language, its own laws and its own stories about how the world began.

About a thousand years ago, Norse sailors from Greenland reached the coast of Newfoundland, in what is now Canada. They built a small settlement, which archaeologists found in the 1960s, but it did not last long.
In October 1492 Columbus reached an island in the Caribbean Sea, where the Taino people lived. To the Europeans the land was new, but to the Taino it had always been home.

The newcomers carried diseases such as smallpox and measles, which had never reached the Americas before. People had built up no protection against them, and the illnesses often spread faster than the Europeans did.
Historians disagree about how many people died, but in many regions the loss was enormous. Some scholars suggest that, in the worst-hit places, as many as nine in ten people died within a century.

In 1519 a Spanish commander named Hernan Cortes marched toward Tenochtitlan with several hundred soldiers. He succeeded because thousands of local warriors, who resented Aztec rule, joined him, and because smallpox then struck the city.

The Inca empire was already weakened by smallpox and a civil war between two brothers. When Francisco Pizarro arrived in 1532, his small force captured the ruler Atahualpa, and the empire began to collapse.

When so many farmers died, forests slowly grew back across the fields they had cleared. Some scientists think this removed carbon dioxide from the air and cooled the climate a little, but others disagree.
New tools are changing what we know about the early Americas, and the discoveries keep coming. Lasers flown above forests reveal hidden ruins, while DNA tests help to trace where people came from.
The first peoples of the Americas did not disappear, and their descendants live in every country. Many millions still speak languages such as Quechua, Nahuatl, Guarani and the Mayan languages.
The story of the Americas did not begin in 1492, and it did not end then either. Every day, people around the world eat foods such as potatoes, maize, tomatoes and chocolate that first grew there.
C1C2: In the year before Columbus set sail, the Americas were home to tens of millions of people who spoke hundreds of languages and lived in very different kinds of societies. Scholars still argue about the exact numbers, because the evidence is scattered and the later collapse of so many peoples makes counting difficult. This is the story of those peoples and of the world they had built over many thousands of years.

Sometime more than fifteen thousand years ago, and perhaps much earlier, small groups of hunters from northeastern Asia began to move into the Americas. Scientists still debate the exact date and the route, because ancient footprints and tools are hard to find and harder to date, but many think that some people travelled by boat along the Pacific coast. Their descendants would eventually reach every corner of two continents, from the Arctic to the southern tip of South America.

Along the Pacific coast, the travellers could have found a chain of rich feeding grounds, with kelp forests, seals, fish and shellfish all within reach of a small boat. Many scientists think that this ribbon of food allowed families to move south quickly, perhaps faster than they could have walked across the inland country, which was still covered in ice in places. We may never find the evidence for certain, however, because the old coastlines now lie under the sea.

The Americas then held some astonishing animals, among them mammoths, giant ground sloths that stood taller than a man, and huge bears that could look a rider in the eye. Within a few thousand years most of them had gone, and scientists continue to debate whether the cause was a warming climate, hunting by people, or, most likely, some combination of the two. The loss changed the continents for ever, and the survivors had to learn to live in a different kind of world.

As the climate warmed and the ice retreated, the descendants of the first travellers spread into almost every kind of country, from rainforest and desert to high mountain valleys and frozen coasts. Each community learned its own landscape in detail, and over many centuries they developed hundreds of languages, many unrelated to one another, and a vast variety of customs. It is a mistake, therefore, to speak of Native Americans as if they were a single people with a single way of life.

In what is now southern Mexico, farmers began, perhaps nine thousand years ago, to save and plant the seeds of a wild grass called teosinte, whose few small kernels bore little resemblance to a modern ear of corn. Generation after generation of patient selection transformed it into maize, one of the most productive and adaptable crops that humans have ever created. It was a feat of plant breeding that remains remarkable today, and it would eventually feed people on every continent.

In many regions, farmers planted maize, beans and squash together, a combination that suited the three plants and their growers equally well. The beans climbed the maize stalks and added nitrogen to the soil, the broad squash leaves shaded the ground and discouraged weeds, and together the three crops gave people a diet that was balanced in energy and protein. Few agricultural systems anywhere in the world show such elegant cooperation between different species.

Farmers in the Americas developed an extraordinary range of food plants, among them potatoes, tomatoes, chillies, peanuts, pumpkins, vanilla, sunflowers and cacao, the source of chocolate. Before 1492, none of these was grown in Europe, Africa or Asia, so that Italian cooking without tomatoes and Indian cooking without chillies are both surprisingly recent ideas. It is hard to imagine the modern world's kitchens without the work of those early plant breeders.

High in the Andes, herders raised llamas to carry goods over the mountain trails and alpacas for their fine, warm wool, while turkeys in Mexico and guinea pigs in the Andes were raised for meat. The continents had no horses, cattle, sheep or pigs, because the native horses had died out thousands of years earlier, and so most heavy work depended on human muscle. Wheels were known as toys, but with no animals strong enough to pull a cart, they were never put to everyday use.

In the dry coastal valley of Supe, in Peru, the ruins of Caral show that people were building monumental cities in the Americas about five thousand years ago, at roughly the same time as the first Egyptian pyramids. Its great platforms and sunken plazas were raised without metal tools, and its people traded with coastal and inland communities. Archaeologists find it remarkable that such a city thrived before pottery was in use.

More than three thousand years ago, the Olmec people built towns and ceremonial centres in the hot, wet lowlands near the Gulf of Mexico, and they carved colossal stone heads that still stand as symbols of their skill. Some of the heads are taller than a man, and since the stone came from mountains many kilometres away, moving it must have required enormous organisation. Many later Mexican peoples borrowed Olmec ideas, which is why historians often call it a mother culture, although some prefer to see it as one among several early influences.

Long before Europeans had seen rubber, the peoples of Mesoamerica were tapping the sap of rubber trees, mixing it with the juice of morning glory vines and shaping it into balls that bounced. They played a fast, hard game with them in long stone courts, wearing padded belts to protect their hips, and the contest was linked to religious beliefs about the sun, the moon and the underworld. In some places the game may have ended in sacrifice, though the evidence is limited and scholars debate how common it was.

Between about 250 and 900, the Maya raised dozens of cities across the rainforests and limestone plains of Mexico and Central America, among them Tikal, Palenque and Copan. Each city had its own king, its own temples and its own rivalries, so the Maya world was less a single empire than a restless network of kingdoms that traded, married and fought. At its height, a city like Tikal may have held tens of thousands of people.

The Maya developed a complete writing system in which signs stood for words and syllables, and they carved the deeds of their kings on stone and painted books of folded bark paper, only a handful of which have survived. Their mathematicians worked with the idea of zero, and their astronomers calculated the cycles of the sun, the moon and Venus with astonishing accuracy, building calendars that could predict eclipses. Much of the writing was not understood until the late twentieth century, when scholars finally learned to read it.

Between about 800 and 900, many of the great cities of the southern lowlands lost their rulers, stopped building monuments and gradually emptied, a collapse that has fascinated historians ever since. Droughts, wars and the strain of feeding large populations from thin soils all seem to have played a part, but experts continue to argue about their relative weight. The Maya themselves did not disappear, for the northern cities carried on, and millions of their descendants still speak Mayan languages today.

Not far from today's Mexico City, the great city of Teotihuacan was laid out on a grid, with a wide central avenue running between enormous pyramids dedicated to the sun and the moon. By about the year 500 it probably held more than one hundred thousand people, which made it one of the largest cities anywhere in the world at that time. Strangely, we do not even know what its builders called themselves, since the name Teotihuacan was given centuries later by the Aztecs.

Some two thousand years ago, the Nazca people of southern Peru cleared the dark surface stones from the desert floor to reveal pale ground beneath, creating giant pictures of birds, monkeys, plants and long straight lines. The designs are so vast that they can be understood fully only from the air, and their purpose is still debated, though many scholars think they were connected with water and ritual. Meanwhile, to the north, the Moche people were building adobe pyramids and making superb portrait pottery.

From a modest base at Cusco, high in the Peruvian Andes, the Inca expanded rapidly in the fifteenth century, especially under the ruler Pachacuti, until their realm stretched for thousands of kilometres along the western side of South America. They called it Tawantinsuyu, which means the four parts together, and it may have held ten million people or more. All this was achieved in less than a hundred years, and it ended only a few decades after it had reached its greatest size.

The Inca linked their mountainous empire with a network of roads that ran for tens of thousands of kilometres, climbing cliffs by stone stairways and crossing gorges on bridges woven from grass ropes. Along these roads, relay runners called chasqui passed messages from station to station, so that news could cross a huge distance in a few days. People travelled on foot, with llamas carrying the goods, because there were no horses or wheeled carts.

Instead of an alphabet, the Inca used the quipu, a bundle of coloured cords on which knots of different kinds recorded numbers, such as the grain in a storehouse or the people in a village. Specially trained officials could read these cords, and some scholars suspect that certain quipus also preserved stories or other information beyond numbers, though no one has yet decoded them. It remains one of the most unusual and puzzling recording systems ever devised by any people.

Around 1450, the Inca raised Machu Picchu on a narrow ridge nearly two and a half thousand metres above sea level, probably as a country estate for their ruler. Its walls are built of granite blocks cut so precisely that they fit together without mortar, a method that helps them survive in a region of frequent earthquakes. The terraces on the surrounding slopes prevented landslides and grew crops, making the whole site a masterpiece of practical engineering.

The Inca economy worked without money, markets or coins, for the state asked its subjects to pay their taxes in labour, which was called the mita, by farming state fields, building roads, weaving cloth or serving in the army. In return, the government filled enormous storehouses with food and cloth and shared them out in bad years, so that families in some regions may have been better protected against famine than many peasants in Europe. It was a remarkably organised system, though it demanded a great deal from ordinary families.

The Mexica, whom we usually call the Aztecs, founded their capital Tenochtitlan around 1325 on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco, where the valley's rivers gathered. By 1500 it had grown into a splendid city of temples, palaces and canals, joined to the shore by long causeways, and its population was perhaps two hundred thousand people. That made it larger than almost any city in Europe at the time, and the Spanish soldiers who first saw it wrote that it seemed like something out of an enchanted story.

To feed so large a population, farmers built chinampas, narrow artificial plots made by piling up mud and water plants in the shallow parts of the lake and fencing them with willow trees. The soil was constantly moist and enriched by canal mud, so a single plot could produce several harvests a year, and some chinampas are still farmed near Mexico City today. They are often called floating gardens, but in reality they were fixed to the lake bed.

The market of Tlatelolco, beside Tenochtitlan, astonished the Spanish soldiers who saw it, for it offered food, cloth, feathers, pottery, gold and many other goods, all under the eyes of officials who checked the weights and settled disputes. Cacao beans served as a kind of small change, and cotton cloaks were used for larger payments. One Spanish writer said that tens of thousands of people came on a busy day, a figure that is probably exaggerated but that shows how impressed visitors were.

The Aztec state took education unusually seriously, for most boys attended a local school where they learned military skills, history, songs and the duties of citizenship. The sons of nobles went to a separate college that trained priests, officials and army commanders, while girls usually learned their duties at home, although many also attended schools attached to temples, and some women became priestesses or respected healers. In a world where few ordinary people anywhere could read, such schooling gave Aztec society its confidence and cohesion.

Aztec religion rested on the belief that the gods had given their own blood to bring the world into being, and that the sun would keep moving across the sky only if people returned the gift. This belief led to human sacrifice, a practice that archaeology confirms, though the Spanish, who wanted to justify their conquest, almost certainly exaggerated the numbers. A fair view must also remember that many European states of the same period put people to death in public and in cruel ways.

Near the Mississippi River, in what is now the state of Illinois, the city of Cahokia grew rapidly after about 1050, and at its height it held perhaps ten to twenty thousand people, with many more living in nearby villages. Its largest earth mound, built basket by basket from millions of loads of soil, is wider at the base than Egypt's Great Pyramid and still rises about thirty metres above the plain. Cahokia faded after 1300, and historians are still unsure whether floods, drought, war or disease was to blame.

Between about 850 and 1150, the ancestors of today's Pueblo peoples built a remarkable group of great houses in Chaco Canyon, in the high desert of New Mexico, some of them five storeys tall and containing hundreds of rooms. Careful builders aligned some of the walls and windows with the sun and the moon, and straight roads ran out from the canyon across the desert for many kilometres. The Pueblo people still regard Chaco as a sacred place, and their oral traditions form an important part of how it is understood.

In the woodlands of what is now New York State, five nations, the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca, joined to form the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. The date of its founding is uncertain, but it probably lies between the twelfth and the fifteenth centuries, and the Great Law of Peace set out how clan mothers chose leaders and how councils reached decisions, giving women real political influence. Some historians believe that its ideas influenced later thinking about government in North America, though that claim is still debated.

Along the rainy northwest coast, from Alaska to Oregon, peoples such as the Haida and the Tlingit built rich and complicated societies without farming. The rivers produced huge runs of salmon that could be smoked and stored for the winter. Skilled carpenters used red cedar to make plank houses, ocean-going canoes and tall carved poles that recorded the histories of families, and great feasts called potlatches marked important events and shared wealth. These were prosperous communities with strict ranks and artists of exceptional skill, and their art is admired around the world today.

In the Arctic, where farming was impossible, the Inuit and their ancestors devised some of the cleverest technologies ever invented. Among them were the kayak, the toggling harpoon, sewn skin clothing that kept out the cold, and the snow house, which could be built in a few hours. They hunted seals, whales and caribou with an intimate knowledge of the ice, the weather and the animals' habits. Survival in such a place was never luck but the fruit of knowledge passed from one generation to the next.

On the Great Plains, millions of bison once roamed the grass, and peoples such as the Blackfoot and the Pawnee built their lives around them. They used the meat for food, the hides for clothing and tents, and the bones for tools. Until horses arrived with the Spanish, the hunters worked on foot, cooperating to drive herds into traps or over cliffs. Horses came later and changed the Plains way of life enormously, but that is a story that begins only after 1492.

Recent discoveries suggest that the Amazon rainforest was not an untouched wilderness but home to many farming communities, some with large villages joined by roads and ditches. Peoples there enriched poor soil by mixing in charcoal, bones and broken pottery, producing the dark fertile earth called terra preta. They also planted useful trees such as Brazil nut and peach palm, so that parts of the forest were effectively a garden. How many people lived there, and how large their settlements grew, are questions that scientists are still working to answer.

Across North America in particular, many peoples deliberately set low fires every year or two, which cleared brush, returned nutrients to the soil, and encouraged the berries, grasses and young shoots that attracted deer and other game. The result was a landscape that early European visitors described as open and park-like, and that they mistook for natural wilderness. Much of what looked wild to the newcomers had in fact been tended for thousands of years.

Trade networks carried goods across enormous distances, so that blue turquoise from the American Southwest has been found in the ruins of Mexican cities, and shells from the Pacific have been found far inland. Obsidian, a volcanic glass that could be chipped into razor-sharp blades, was traded for hundreds of kilometres in many regions, and cacao beans moved north from the tropics. These routes, often followed on foot or by canoe, show that no community lived in isolation.

High in the Andes, where frost can strike any night of the year, farmers invented a way of turning the potato into chuno. They let the tubers freeze overnight, trampled out the water and dried them in the thin, sunny air. The result was light, easy to carry and able to last for years, so it could be stored against bad harvests and carried along the great roads to feed armies and workers. They also grew thousands of varieties of potato, a diversity that still astonishes botanists.

Because a good harvest depended on planting at the right moment, the peoples of the Americas became careful observers of the sky. They built towers, walls and temples that marked the rising of the sun at the solstices and the movements of the moon and planets. Inca priests watched the sun from the hills around Cusco, for example, while the Maya raised a round observatory at Chichen Itza. Their calendars were practical tools as much as expressions of belief, for they told whole communities when to sow, when to harvest and when to hold their festivals.

Craftspeople in the Americas worked in an astonishing range of materials. They wove cloth so fine that it amazed the first Europeans who saw it, hammered gold and silver into jewellery and masks, and arranged the brilliant feathers of tropical birds into cloaks and headdresses. For the Inca, the finest cloth was worth more than gold, and it was given as a precious gift to loyal officials. Such objects were not decoration only, but also signs of rank, belief and wealth.

Some peoples lived under powerful emperors, others in confederacies governed by councils, and others in small bands that made decisions by discussion and kept no rulers at all. Hundreds of languages were spoken, belonging to dozens of unrelated families, and the differences between them were at least as great as those among the languages of Europe and Asia. That is why historians prefer to speak of many peoples and nations, each with its own history, rather than of a single group.

Around the year 1000, some five hundred years before Columbus, Norse sailors from Greenland crossed the cold sea to the island of Newfoundland, in what is now Canada. They built a small camp of turf-walled buildings at a place called L'Anse aux Meadows. Archaeologists uncovered it in the 1960s, and tree rings in the wood found there now fix a firm date for the Norse presence. The settlement was abandoned after only a short time, however, so the contact had no lasting effect on either side.

In October 1492, Columbus and his crews came ashore on a small island in the Bahamas, where they were met by the Taino, a people who farmed cassava and sweet potatoes, wove cotton and travelled between islands in large canoes. For the Europeans it was a discovery, but for the Taino it was simply their home, and within a few decades their communities on the larger islands would be devastated. The meeting of the two worlds had begun, and neither would ever be the same again.

The Europeans carried diseases such as smallpox, measles and influenza, which had been unknown in the Americas, and a people who had never met them had no immunity and died in terrible numbers. Epidemics often travelled along trade routes ahead of the newcomers, so that some communities were struck by disease before they had ever seen a European. In many regions, villages lost so many people that fields went untended and the survivors could not carry on their old ways of life.

Scholars cannot say exactly how many people died, because the early records are thin and the estimates of the original population vary so widely, but most agree that the loss was one of the greatest disasters in human history. In some regions the population may have fallen by as much as nine in ten within a century, and whole languages and traditions disappeared with it. Those who survived rebuilt their communities in a world that had been overturned, and their descendants remember that history today.

In 1519 Hernan Cortes led about five hundred Spanish soldiers inland toward Tenochtitlan, and along the way he gained thousands of allies from peoples who resented the heavy tribute that the Aztecs demanded. Smallpox then swept through the city in 1520, killing many of its people and leaders, and after a long siege the capital fell in 1521. The Spanish soldiers could not have won alone, and the conquest was as much the work of local allies and disease as of weapons.

Smallpox had probably reached the Andes ahead of the Spanish, killing the Inca ruler Huayna Capac and igniting a bitter civil war between his sons Atahualpa and Huascar. When Francisco Pizarro arrived with fewer than two hundred men in 1532, he seized Atahualpa by surprise and held him for ransom, and the empire began to fall apart. The Inca continued to resist from the mountains for another forty years, which shows how fiercely the people fought to keep their independence.

As the farmers vanished, forest began to spread across fields, orchards and clearings that had once been cultivated. Some researchers believe that the new trees absorbed so much carbon dioxide that they helped to cool the global climate in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The idea is a striking one, although many scientists remain unconvinced that the effect was large enough to be measured. It reminds us, whatever its outcome, that events in one part of the world can leave traces in the atmosphere of the whole planet.

New technology is changing what we know about the early Americas almost every year. Lidar surveys, which use laser pulses fired from aircraft to see through the leaves, have revealed tens of thousands of hidden Maya buildings, roads and fields in Guatemala. DNA studies are tracing the movements of the first peoples, while tree rings and soil samples record changes in the climate. Meanwhile, the oral histories kept by Indigenous communities are increasingly treated as valuable evidence alongside the work of archaeologists.

The first peoples of the Americas did not vanish, and their descendants, numbering tens of millions, live today in every country of both continents. Millions of them speak languages such as Quechua, Nahuatl, Guarani and the many Mayan tongues, and they keep alive farming methods, festivals, crafts and stories that stretch back thousands of years. They have also created modern cities, universities and governments, and many are working to protect their languages and their land.

The history of the Americas did not begin with Columbus, for these were lands of cities, farms, observatories and nations long before 1492. Their gifts to the world, including maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chocolate and rubber, are with us every day, and their descendants remain among us. To know that older story is to see the whole world, and the people who live in it, a little more fairly.
